content.title: About
content.content: Bread with oat bran is a whole‑grain loaf that contains oat bran (2532). The bran gives the bread a nutty aroma, higher nutritional value and a dense crumb. It is suitable for breakfasts, snacks and as a base for sandwiches.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oat bran is the outer layer of the oat grain, rich in fiber and beta‑glucan.
Bread with bran is often used in dietetic nutrition because of its low glycemic index.
Bran helps regulate blood sugar levels and promotes satiety.
Oat bran can be obtained from whole oats or as a by‑product of oat processing.
In some countries oat‑bran bread is a traditional staple of rural cuisine.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Bran provides both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion and gut microbiota.

items.title: Lowers cholesterol
items.content: Beta‑glucan from oat bran can reduce intestinal cholesterol absorption.

items.title: Supports blood sugar control
items.content: Fiber slows glucose absorption, helping to stabilize blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Bran contains thiamine, niacin and folate, essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The bread supplies magnesium, iron and zinc, important for muscle function and immunity.

items.title: High fiber content
items.content: Large portions may cause bloating, gas or diarrhea in people with sensitive digestive systems.

items.title: Oat allergy
items.content: Rare, but possible allergic reactions in individuals sensitive to oats.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Phytates can reduce the absorption of certain minerals; pairing with vitamin‑C‑rich foods is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the bread plain, as toast, for sandwiches, or with soups. It pairs well with honey, nut butter, cheese, avocado or cottage cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the loaf in a cool, dry place in a paper bag or container. For longer storage, freeze it and thaw at room temperature before use.

content.title: About
content.content: Corned beef patty is a ready‑to‑eat beef patty that has been cured in a seasoned brine. It has a firm texture, a rich meaty flavor and a slightly salty aroma typical of traditional corned beef.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional corned beef is cured in a brine with nitrites that preserve its pink color.
Patty format is convenient for quick meals – just heat on a pan or in the microwave.
In the United States corned beef is often served as a sandwich with sauerkraut and mustard.
The brine may contain mustard, cloves, bay leaf and brown sugar.
Beef patty retains most of the protein and iron found in whole meat.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Corned beef patty provides high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Beef is a good source of heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The patty contains vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Suitable for low‑carb diets as it supplies protein without significant carbs.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc in beef supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The brine makes the patty fairly salty; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Nitrites
items.content: Some recipes use nitrites to preserve color; excess intake may be undesirable.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may be allergic to beef.

items.title: Potential bacterial contamination
items.content: As with any meat product, proper storage and thorough cooking are required.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the patty in a skillet, oven or microwave. It is often served in a sandwich with bread, sauerkraut and mustard, or diced for salads and quick‑cook dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the patty refrigerated at 0 °C–4 °C in its original packaging. Once opened, consume within 3–5 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag for up to 3 months. Ensure the product is fully heated before eating.

green-peas-fresh-cooked-with-butter-or-m.title: Green peas, fresh, cooked with butter or margarine

content.title: About
content.content: Green peas are young pods of the pea plant (Pisum sativum) harvested before the seeds fully mature. Cooking them with butter or margarine gives a delicate flavor, keeps the bright green color, and creates a tender texture. Peas are often served as a side dish or added to salads, soups, and stews.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green peas are one of the oldest cultivated crops, grown for more than 5,000 years.
They contain more protein than most vegetables and are comparable to other legumes.
Peas can fix atmospheric nitrogen, improving soil fertility.
In many countries green peas are traditionally served as a buttery puree.
There are over 100 varieties of green peas, differing in size, flavor, and harvest time.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: One cup of cooked peas provides about 8 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, helps regulate blood sugar, and promotes satiety.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Peas contain B1, B6, and folate, which are important for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Contains vitamin C and antioxidants
items.content: Vitamin C supports immunity, while antioxidants protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Minerals: iron, magnesium, potassium
items.content: These minerals contribute to blood formation, muscle function, and fluid balance.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to legumes, including peas.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Oligosaccharides can cause bloating in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sodium content in added butter/margarine
items.content: When using salted butter or margarine, monitor overall sodium intake.

items.title: Food safety
items.content: Raw or undercooked beans may contain phytic acid, but proper cooking with butter eliminates the concern.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Peas can be served as a side, tossed into salads, soups, stews, or mashed into a puree. For butter‑cooked peas, sauté them for 5‑7 minutes over medium heat, then season with a pinch of salt and freshly ground black pepper.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh peas in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 5 days. Cooked or sautéed peas should be refrigerated and consumed within 3 days; for longer storage, freeze them in a sealed bag.

ham-sandwich-on-wheat-with-cheese.title: Ham sandwich on wheat bread with cheese

content.title: About
content.content: A ham sandwich on wheat bread with cheese is a classic sandwich that layers slices of ham and melted cheese between two pieces of whole‑grain wheat bread. It is commonly served in cafés, cafeterias, and as a quick snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wheat bread provides complex carbohydrates that sustain energy levels.
Ham is a source of easily digestible protein and vitamin B12.
Cheese adds calcium and a creamy flavor.
Ham‑and‑cheese sandwiches are popular in the US and Europe as convenient lunch options.
The combination is often featured in school menus because of its simplicity.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Ham and cheese together supply a substantial amount of complete protein needed for tissue repair.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Cheese provides calcium that supports bone and dental health.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Ham contains vitamin B6 and B12, which aid normal nervous system function.

items.title: Steady energy
items.content: Wheat bread delivers slow‑release carbs, helping maintain satiety.

items.title: Potential probiotic benefit
items.content: If whole‑grain sourdough bread is used, it may contribute to a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Processed ham often contains high levels of salt, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Cheese and ham can be high in saturated fat, so intake should be limited for heart‑health concerns.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to casein found in cheese.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: Commercial ham may contain nitrites and other preservatives that should be considered with frequent consumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich can be eaten cold or lightly toasted. Add lettuce, tomato, or mustard for extra flavor and texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the assembled sandwich in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Keep ham and cheese wrapped separately to maintain freshness.

content.title: About
content.content: Slim Fast nutritional powder is a ready‑to‑drink meal replacement that provides a balanced blend of protein, carbohydrates, vitamins, and minerals. Designed for weight management and sustained energy, it easily dissolves in water or milk.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Slim Fast was first launched in the United States in the 1970s as part of a weight‑loss program.
The powder is available in several flavors, including chocolate, vanilla, and strawberry.
Each serving contains about 200 kcal, making it a convenient low‑calorie meal substitute.
The product has undergone clinical studies confirming its effectiveness when used as part of a diet plan.

items.title: Balanced nutrition
items.content: Provides essential macronutrients – protein, complex carbs, and a modest amount of fat – helping to keep you feeling full.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Fortified with B‑vitamins, vitamin C, iron, calcium, and other micronutrients important for metabolism.

items.title: Calorie control
items.content: Low‑calorie formula allows reduction of daily caloric intake without excessive hunger.

items.title: Convenient usage
items.content: Quickly dissolves in liquid, making it practical for busy lifestyles.

items.title: Supports muscle mass
items.content: Contains about 10 g of protein per serving, aiding muscle preservation during weight loss.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: May contain dairy proteins, soy, or gluten – avoid if you have relevant allergies.

items.title: Low fiber content
items.content: The powder does not replace whole fruits and vegetables, so additional fiber intake is recommended.

items.title: Not suitable for prolonged exclusive use
items.content: Long‑term reliance on meal replacements alone can lead to nutrient deficiencies without proper monitoring.

items.title: Possible gastrointestinal discomfort
items.content: Some individuals may experience bloating or mild stomach upset when switching quickly to meal replacements.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mix one serving (approximately 30 g) of powder with 250 ml of water, milk, or a plant‑based beverage. Stir until fully dissolved and consume immediately. For added flavor and fiber, you may blend in fruit or berries.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the lid tightly sealed to prevent moisture ingress. Refer to the expiration date on the packaging.

content.title: About
content.content: Pork, chop, stuffed is a cut of pork loin that is butterflied, pounded to about 1.5 cm thickness, filled with a mixture of breadcrumbs, herbs, spices and sometimes cheese, then baked or pan‑seared until golden. The dish combines tender meat with a flavorful stuffing.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Stuffed pork chops are popular in European and American cuisines, especially in the US where they are often called “stuffed pork chops”.
Traditional fillings may include apples, cranberries or dried fruit, giving a sweet‑tart note.
Chops are cut from the loin, one of the most tender pork sections.
Proper stuffing helps keep the meat juicy and prevents it from drying out.
Some recipes use Parmesan‑enhanced breadcrumbs for an extra crunchy crust.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Pork provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains thiamine, niacin and vitamin B6, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Pork supplies iron, zinc and selenium, important for immunity and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Stuffed chops contain virtually no carbs, making them suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Beneficial fats
items.content: Lean portions contain monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Fatty cuts can raise cholesterol levels if consumed in excess.

items.title: Food‑borne infection risk
items.content: Undercooked pork may harbor salmonella or trichinella; cook to an internal temperature of 71 °C.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to pork.

items.title: Sodium in the stuffing
items.content: Prepared sauces or salty ingredients in the filling can increase sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Stuff the chops with a blend of breadcrumbs, herbs, garlic and spices, then bake at 180 °C for 25‑30 minutes or pan‑sear until golden. Serve with roasted vegetables, mashed potatoes or a fresh salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw stuffed chops in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in a vacuum‑sealed bag for up to 3 months. Thaw in the fridge, and cooked chops should be refrigerated and eaten within 1 day.

content.title: About
content.content: Mashed potato from fast food is a ready‑to‑eat side dish made from boiled potatoes that are mashed to a smooth consistency and typically enriched with butter, milk, and salt. It is served hot alongside burgers, chicken nuggets, and other fast‑food items.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fast‑food mashed potatoes are usually made from high‑starch potato varieties to achieve a fluffy texture.
In the United States, more than 30 % of all restaurant potato sales are mashed potatoes.
To speed up service, many chains use pre‑blended mixes stored in chilled units and prepared in 2–3 minutes.
Mashed potatoes can be offered in classic buttery flavor or with cheese, garlic, or herb variations.

items.title: Rich in potassium
items.content: Potatoes are a good source of potassium, which supports normal heart and muscle function.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.content: Mashed potatoes retain some vitamin C, an antioxidant important for immune health.

items.title: Quick energy
items.content: Starch provides readily available carbohydrates that fuel the body quickly.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: When made from whole‑potato varieties, a modest amount of fiber remains, aiding digestion.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: The smooth texture makes it suitable for children and people with chewing difficulties.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Fast‑food versions are often heavily salted, which can contribute to elevated blood pressure if consumed frequently.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: Added butter and milk increase calories, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Individuals with lactose intolerance or milk allergy should choose dairy‑free versions.

items.title: Trans‑fat presence
items.content: Some pre‑made mixes may contain partially hydrogenated oils; checking the ingredient list is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the mash hot as a side to meat, chicken, or fish dishes. It can be topped with cheese, fresh herbs, garlic sauce, or seasonings of choice. For a healthier option, select versions without added butter or excess salt.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store prepared mash in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 3 months. Reheat to at least 60 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Quinoa (Chenopodium quinoa) is a seed from the Andes of South America that is cooked and eaten like a grain, although it is not a true cereal. The tiny round seeds come in white, red, and black varieties and have a mild, nutty flavor and a fluffy texture with a slight pop. Quinoa is naturally gluten-free and used in salads, bowls, soups, and side dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Quinoa has been grown in the Andes for thousands of years and was a sacred crop of the Inca.
It is a pseudocereal related to beets, spinach, and chard, not to wheat or rice.
Quinoa is a complete protein, containing all nine essential amino acids.
Quinoa seeds are coated with natural bitter saponins, which should be rinsed off before cooking.
Quinoa cooks in about 15 minutes and the seeds unwind into little tails when done.

items.title: Complete plant protein
items.content: Quinoa provides all essential amino acids, which is unusual for a plant food.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Quinoa contributes fiber that supports digestion and fullness.

items.title: Provides magnesium, manganese, and folate
items.content: These nutrients support muscle function, metabolism, and cell function.

items.title: Provides iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals support oxygen transport and immune function.

items.title: Naturally gluten-free
items.content: Quinoa suits people who avoid gluten, provided it is processed safely.

items.title: Saponins
items.content: The natural coating on quinoa tastes bitter and may irritate some people's stomachs, so rinse quinoa well before cooking.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Quinoa contains oxalates, which people prone to kidney stones may need to limit.

items.title: Allergic reactions and digestion
items.content: Quinoa allergy is uncommon but can occur, and large amounts of fiber may cause gas or bloating.

items.title: Gluten cross-contamination
items.content: People with celiac disease should choose quinoa labeled gluten-free.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Rinse quinoa in a fine strainer and simmer it in about twice its volume of water until the seeds are tender, then fluff with a fork. Use it in salads, bowls, soups, stuffed vegetables, porridge, and patties, or as a rice substitute. Toasting the rinsed seeds briefly before cooking deepens the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry quinoa in an airtight container in a cool, dry place, where it keeps for a year or longer. Cooked quinoa should be refrigerated in an airtight container and eaten within three to five days, or frozen.
